name: Indian Yellow
poem: A glowing amber yellow shipped in dirty balls from Bengal — whose source nobody in Europe could explain, until the chemists figured out it was cow urine.

recipe.note: A warm amber yellow, golden and slightly orange.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: A transparent golden yellow with extraordinary glowing properties — the favourite of every painter who needed sunset light.

entries.title: Rain, Steam and Speed
entries.blurb: The glowing yellow steam of Turner's locomotive is Indian yellow, glazed thin over white — a colour Turner stockpiled by the pound and used compulsively.

entries.title: Rajasthani Miniatures
entries.blurb: The pigment originated in India, where it had been used for centuries before European traders noticed — for the gold of palace domes and saffron robes.

entries.title: Vermeer's Studio Window
entries.blurb: The honey-yellow light streaming through Vermeer's leaded windows is often Indian yellow over lead-white — the colour of Delft in late afternoon.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: The colour of celebration and renunciation, depending on which side of the world is wearing it.

entries.title: The Sikh Turban
entries.blurb: The kesari (saffron) turban worn by initiated Sikhs is exactly the warm Indian yellow — a colour of sacrifice and willingness to die for the faith.

entries.title: The Saree
entries.blurb: Mustard and amber Indian-yellow sarees — particularly in cotton — were the everyday dress of much of rural India, and remain prized for their warmth on dark skin.

entries.title: Buddhist Monastic Robes
entries.blurb: Monk's robes are dyed with turmeric and saffron — a yellow close to Indian yellow, deliberately worn to make the wearer humble, visible, accountable.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: The pigment's source was an open secret in India and an unsolved mystery in Europe for over a century.

entries.title: Mango-Fed Cows
entries.blurb: The pigment was concentrated from the urine of cows fed exclusively on mango leaves and water — a diet that made the animals sickly and the pigment phosphorescent.

entries.title: The Marigold
entries.blurb: The same Indian yellow appears in marigold flowers, strung by the kilometre into garlands for temples and weddings — a colour of welcome.

entries.title: The Golden Hour
entries.blurb: The exact warm gold of the half hour before sunset — every photographer's favourite colour, exactly the hue Turner was chasing with his Indian-yellow brushes.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: After India's animal-welfare laws made true Indian yellow extinct, the colour name carried on — attached to chemistry it never knew.

entries.title: The New York Cab
entries.blurb: John Hertz chose taxi-cab yellow because a University of Chicago study said it was the most visible colour from a distance — a synthetic Indian yellow, mass produced.

entries.title: Yellow Submarine
entries.blurb: The animated Beatles film's signature yellow is closer to Indian yellow than to lemon — a deliberate choice for warmth and psychedelic resonance.

entries.title: Coldplay's "Yellow"
entries.blurb: Chris Martin says he wrote the song under a yellow streetlight outside a studio in Wales — the colour came first, the lyric followed.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Like many pigments shipped through colonial trade, Indian yellow's names tell the story of who was selling it and who was buying.

entries.title: "Peori"
entries.blurb: The original Indian name — simply meaning "yellow." The pigment was indistinguishable from the colour, in everyday Bihar speech.

entries.title: "Purée"
entries.blurb: The dirty yellow balls that arrived in London colour shops were called "purée" — a French-sounding euphemism for what was, factually, dehydrated cow urine.

entries.title: "Banned, 1908"
entries.blurb: Animal-cruelty laws ended the trade — the cows were dying. The pigment vanished from the market within five years, replaced by synthetic azo dyes.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Indian yellow's cultural weight outlived its chemistry — the colour kept its meanings even after its source disappeared.

entries.title: Sannyasa
entries.blurb: The saffron-yellow robe of the Hindu renunciant — and the same yellow of the rising sun, marking the colour of a new beginning, every day.

entries.title: Solar Sovereignty
entries.blurb: Mughal emperors had themselves painted with golden haloes in Indian yellow — borrowing solar imagery from the Hindu tradition they ruled over.

entries.title: Joy
entries.blurb: Yellow is the most cross-culturally consistent colour for joy — Western, Indian, Chinese, African colour studies all return roughly the same answer.
